title: The Circle Deming Disowned
subtitle: An American statistician taught Japanese managers to work in a circle. They turned his idea into Plan–Do–Check–Act — and he spent his last years saying they had got the name wrong.

card.essence: Don't make a big change in one go. Plan a small change, try it, check what happened, then act on what you learnt — and go round again.

intention: you'll learn how a quality-control idea travelled from America to Japan and back, run a PDCA cycle on a real problem, and practise zero and first conditionals: If you press this, it stops. If the test works, we'll use it everywhere.
warmup: When you try something new at work or at home, do you plan carefully or just start?
Think of a small change that made a big difference to your daily routine. How did you know it worked?
Why do some people find it hard to admit that a plan didn't work?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: Every car was inspected by hand before it left the factory.
items.meaning: inspect — to look at something carefully to check its quality. (nouns inspection, inspector)

items.sent: The school ran a small trial with two classes before changing the timetable for everyone.
items.meaning: trial — a test to see whether something works. (a trial run, trial and error)

items.sent: The hospital wanted to standardise the checklist so that every ward used the same one.
items.meaning: standardise — to make things the same according to a fixed standard. (noun standardisation)

items.sent: The film's title is a corruption of an old local name that nobody uses any more.
items.meaning: corruption — here: a changed, spoiled form of a word or idea. (also: dishonest behaviour by people in power; verb corrupt)

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: hypothesis · feedback · iterate. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (noun) Comments about how well something works, used to improve it.
items.meaning: feedback — “Customer feedback showed that the new design was too heavy.”

items.sent: (verb) To repeat a process, improving it a little each time.
items.meaning: iterate — “We iterated on the design five times before the launch.” (noun iteration)

items.sent: (noun) An idea that might explain something, which you then test.
items.meaning: hypothesis — “Our hypothesis was that shorter meetings would save time.” (plural hypotheses)

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: ___ an experiment  ·  ___ a business  ·  ___ out of time
items.meaning: run — (run an experiment, run a business, run out of time)
control — (quality control, lose control, out of control)

items.sent: ___ a lesson  ·  ___ from your mistakes  ·  ___ by heart
items.meaning: learn — (learn a lesson, learn from your mistakes, learn something by heart)

vocab_use: What have you learnt by trial and error?
When did feedback change your mind about something you'd made or done?
What would you like to standardise at work or at home — and what should never be standardised?

story.heading: Part 1 — A circle, not a line
paras: In the 1920s, Walter Shewhart was working at Bell Telephone Laboratories in the United States, studying how to make factory products more reliable. The usual way of thinking about production was a straight line: write a specification, produce the product, inspect it at the end.

In a book published in 1939, Shewhart argued for something different: “These three steps must go in a circle instead of in a straight line.” Specification, production and inspection, he explained, were like the steps of science — making a hypothesis, carrying out an experiment and testing the hypothesis.
The book was edited by a 39-year-old statistician called W. Edwards Deming. He was going to carry Shewhart's circle to the other side of the world.
checks: What was the usual “straight line” way of thinking?
What did Shewhart compare the three steps to?
answers: Write a specification, produce the product, inspect it at the end.
The steps of science: making a hypothesis, carrying out an experiment and testing it.
story.discuss: In your work or studies, do you work more in straight lines or in circles?

story.heading: Part 2 — The Deming wheel
paras: In 1950, Deming taught an eight-day seminar on quality control for Japanese managers and engineers, organised by the Japanese Union of Scientists and Engineers. He turned the straight line of design, produce, sell into a circle by adding a fourth step: redesign through market research. Then round again, and again.

The Japanese called it the “Deming wheel”. Japanese executives then recast it in their own terms as Plan, Do, Check, Act. Nobody knows exactly who did it. As Ronald Moen, who later researched the history of the cycle, wrote: “No one person claimed authorship.”

Together with seven basic quality tools — among them the Pareto chart and the fishbone diagram — PDCA became the foundation of kaizen, the Japanese approach of continuous, step-by-step improvement. They are still used today.
checks: How did Deming change the straight line in 1950?
Who turned the Deming wheel into PDCA?
What did PDCA become part of in Japan?
answers: He added a fourth step — redesign through market research — and made it a circle.
Japanese executives; no one person claimed authorship.
The foundation of kaizen (continuous improvement), together with the seven basic quality tools.
story.discuss: Why do you think nobody claimed to have invented PDCA?

story.heading: Part 3 — Study, not check
paras: You might expect Deming to be pleased. He wasn't. In his four-day seminars in the 1980s he often warned audiences that the word “check” was wrong, because in English it means “to hold back”. What he wanted was not checking but studying — learning from the results.

In 1990, commenting on a manuscript by Moen and two colleagues, he wrote: “be sure to call it PDSA, not the corruption PDCA.” A year later, shown a chart labelled Plan/Do/Check/Act, he replied: “How the PDCA ever came into existence I know not.” His final version, in 1993, was the Shewhart Cycle for Learning and Improvement: Plan, Do, Study, Act.

Deming died at the end of 1993. Today both names are used, often by people who have never heard of the argument. But the difference matters. “Check” asks: did it work? “Study” asks: what did we learn?
checks: Why did Deming dislike the word “check”?
What did he want people to call the cycle?
What is the difference between checking and studying?
answers: Because, he said, in English it means “to hold back”.
Checking asks whether it worked; studying asks what you learnt.
story.discuss: Does the name of a method matter, or only how people use it?

tool_tab.lead: Four steps in a circle. Each turn of the wheel tests one small change, and what you learn becomes the plan for the next turn.
how: Plan: describe the problem, your idea for a change, and what you expect to happen — your prediction.
Do: try the change on a small scale — one team, one week, one shop.
Check (or Study): compare what happened with what you predicted. What surprised you?
Act: keep the change and make it standard, adjust it, or drop it — then plan the next turn.

sort.intro: A café wants shorter queues at lunchtime. Which step of the cycle is each action?

items.text: The manager compares this week's waiting times with last week's.
items.why: comparing the results with what was expected.

items.text: They decide to try a separate counter for takeaway coffee, and predict that queues will be five minutes shorter.
items.why: an idea for a change, plus a prediction.

items.text: For one week, a second barista serves takeaway orders only.
The new counter works, so it becomes the normal way of working in all three cafés.
Staff notice that the takeaway counter was quick, but the main queue was still long because of food orders.
items.why: studying what happened — including the surprise.

items.text: The team agrees exactly what they will measure, and for how long, before anything changes.
items.why: deciding how you will judge the test, before you start.

breaks: The circle stops at Do. Many teams try something and never find out whether it worked.
Too slow for emergencies. In a crisis there may be no time for a careful trial; a faster loop may fit better.
Small tests, big problems. Some changes can't be tested on a small scale — and some results take years to appear.
discuss: Choose a small problem in your life and plan the first turn of the cycle.
Do you agree with Deming that “check” is the wrong word?

cousins.name: The OODA Loop
cousins.text: Another loop — built for speed and competition rather than careful improvement.

cousins.name: The Fishbone Diagram
cousins.text: One of the seven basic quality tools — find the causes before you plan a change.

cousins.name: The Five Whys
cousins.text: Find the root cause first; then test your fix with PDCA.

grammar.name: zero and first conditionals
grammar.lead: PDCA is built on predictions: if we change this, that will happen. English uses two simple conditionals — one for things that are always true, one for real possibilities in the future.
notes:
Zero conditional: if/when + present simple, present simple — for facts and things that always happen.
“If you heat ice, it melts.”  “When the light is red, the machine stops.”

First conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb — for a real possibility in the future.
“If the trial works, we'll use it in every shop.”

Instead of will, you can use may, might, could or an imperative.
“If the results are good, we might expand.”  “If anything goes wrong, call me.”

when or if? When = you're sure it will happen; if = it may or may not.
“When the test ends, we'll look at the data.”  “If the test fails, we'll try again.”
Watch out: no will in the if part: ~~If it will work, we will keep it~~ → “If it works, we'll keep it.”

exercises.heading: Zero or first?
exercises.intro: Put the verbs in brackets into the correct form.
items: 1. If you ___ (not water) plants, they die.
2. If the new rota ___ (reduce) waiting times, we'll keep it.
3. When you ___ (press) this button, the machine starts.
4. If it rains tomorrow, the outdoor test ___ (be) cancelled.
5. We ___ (not know) whether it works if we don't measure it.

exercises.heading: Make a prediction
exercises.intro: You are planning a trial. Complete each prediction in your own words. Possible answers are shown.
items: 1. If we start meetings at 9.30 instead of 9.00, ___
answers: 4. …we'll compare the results with our prediction.

grammar.closing: Now tell your teacher about a small change you'd like to try, with three first conditionals: what you'll do, what you predict, and what you'll do if it fails.

speak.intro: Go round the wheel out loud. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “If we try …, I think … will happen.” · “Let's test it on a small scale first.” · “What did we learn?” · “Next time round, we'll …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — One turn of the wheel
paras: Choose a small problem at work, at home or in your town. Talk it through: Plan, Do, Check, Act.

tasks.label: Task 2 — A change that failed
paras: Describe a change that didn't work. How could a small trial have helped?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Check or study?
paras: Deming said “check” was the wrong word. Explain the difference between checking and studying, with an example from your own life.

final: Why do organisations so often skip the Check step?
Is it possible to improve continuously — or do people need a rest from change?
Deming rejected the name PDCA, but it is still used. Who really owns an idea once it spreads?
From memory: tell the story of the cycle from Shewhart to Deming's PDSA, and make two predictions with if … will.
